study_type.claude: Mixed methods (industrial experience report: online A/B experiments, offline evaluation, qualitative UX studies, observational DiD)
study_type.nlm: Mixed methods (online A/B experiments, observational DiD causal inference, qualitative UX studies)
study_type.note: Claude also frames it as an industrial experience report (workshop paper).

research_method.claude: Industrial experience report: online A/B experiments (2.5K+ users/group for 2 weeks; 10k+ users/group for 1 month), offline evaluation (chrF), qualitative UX studies, observational Difference-in-Differences (Callaway and Sant'Anna) on logs with ~36k treated vs 18k control developers
research_method.nlm: Online A/B experiments (2,500+ and 10,000+ developers per group), offline ChrF evaluation, qualitative UX studies, observational DiD causal inference (Callaway and Sant'Anna) with 36,000 treatment vs 18,000 control developers
research_method.value: Industrial experience report combining online A/B experiments (2,500+ users per group for 2 weeks; 10,000+ per group for 1 month), offline model evaluation (chrF), qualitative UX studies and an observational Difference-in-Differences analysis (Callaway and Sant'Anna) of log-based productivity metrics; ~36k adopters vs ~18k non-adopters; robustness checks (fixed-effect model, stratification)

context.claude: Industry; Google internal IDE and software engineering toolchain; Google engineers (A/B groups 2.5K+ and 10k+ per group; DiD 36k treatment, 18k control)
context.nlm: Industry; Google internal enterprise IDE and toolchain; Google engineers (2,500+ and 10,000+ per A/B group; 36,000 treatment and 18,000 control)
context.value: industry; Google internal IDE and software engineering toolchain (code completion and Transform Code features); Google software engineers: A/B groups of 2,500+ and 10,000+ users, DiD with ~36k treatment and ~18k control developers

data_window.claude: November 2023–December 2024 (DiD analysis window); code-completion metrics over 4 weeks in March 2025
data_window.value: November 2023–December 2024 (DiD analysis window); code-completion metrics over 4 weeks in March 2025

cat_productivity.note: Change List throughput (CLT), Active Coding Time per CL, investigation-session duration, FCML.

cat_quality.note: Borderline: quality of AI suggestions (acceptance rate as quality proxy, offline chrF, edits in unrelated files), not software-product quality.

cat_collaboration.note: Code review appears only in the CL definition.

cat_satisfaction.note: Borderline: both tag acceptance rate as a Satisfaction proxy (paper: proxy for 'user annoyance'); Claude also lists the unspecified 'positive user perception on usefulness'.

cat_activity.note: Characters added per accept, shown suggestions, prompt counts, weekly active users/prompts.

cat_delivery.note: Both tag CLT 'Productivity / Delivery', but it is a throughput measure (CLs submitted per month), not deployment frequency or lead time.

cat_devex.note: NotebookLM tags MeanDurInvSess and review time 'DevEx', but the DevEx framework is not used.

cat_survey.note: Borderline: only an unspecified 'positive user perception on usefulness' and qualitative UX studies used for design; metrics are log-based.

evidence.quote: We evaluate the impact of AI-powered features on productivity through causal inference, both online (A/B tests) and offline (observational causal analysis).
We used observational data on developers' interactions with the feature and the Difference-in-Differences (DiD) causal inference framework, specifically the Callaway and Sant'Anna method [1].
The treatment group ( 36k developers) consisted of users who adopted TC in January-December 2024 and the control group (18k developers) consisted of those who did not adopt it by December 2024.
The data originates from Google's software engineering toolchain.
The analysis window was from November 2023 to December 2024, with pre-adoption months serving as the pre-treatment period.
Cumulatively, with the above improvements, in March 2025 over 4 weeks, we achieved the success metrics presented below
We discuss Google's journey in developing and refining two internal AI-based IDE features: code completion and natural-languagedriven code transformation (Transform Code).
Significant increase (17.5% with 95% confidence interval [15.9%, 19.0%]) in CLT per user-month
while keeping acceptance rate steady, which we treat as a proxy for quality and user annoyance.

Offline evaluation on our curated evaluation dataset-which is a split of the collected rewrites-shows an improvement in the median ChrF score [15] from 84.5 to 88.8, a reduction of edits in unrelated files from 13 to 0.
Fraction of code written by ML (FCML) 28.7% FCML excluding paste in denominator 70.6% Acceptance rate 45% Average characters added per accept 62
